acacia.e: From Latin acacia, from Ancient Greek ἀκακία (akakía, “shittah tree”), either from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”) (compare ἀκή (akḗ, “point”)) or more likely a Pre-Greek word.
acacia.g: A shrub or tree of the tribe Acacieae.

accent.e: From Middle English accent, from Medieval Latin accentus and Old French accent, acent, both from Latin accentus, past participle of accinō (“sing to, sing along”), from ad- + canō (“to sing”). The word accent had been borrowed into Old English already, but was lost and reborrowed in Middle English.
accent.g: A higher-pitched or stronger (louder or longer) articulation of a particular syllable of a word or phrase in order to distinguish it from th

accent.e: From Middle French accenter, from Old French accenter, from Latin accentō, from accentus.
accent.g: To express the accent of vocally; to utter with accent.

accept.e: From Middle English accepten, borrowed from Old French accepter, or directly from Latin acceptō, acceptāre (“receive”), frequentative of accipiō, formed from ad- + capiō (“to take”).
accept.g: To receive, especially with a consent, with favour, or with approval.

acceptable.e: From Middle English acceptable, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French acceptable, from Late Latin acceptābilis (“worthy of acceptance”). Morphologically accept + -able.
acceptable.g: Capable, worthy, or sure of being accepted or received with pleasure; welcome; gratifying; pleasing to a receiver.

acceptably.e: From Middle English acceptably, equivalent to acceptable + -ly.
acceptably.g: In an acceptable manner; in a manner to please or give satisfaction.

acceptance.e: Probably partly from Middle French acceptance (from Old French accepter (“accept”)) and partly from accept + -ance.
acceptance.g: The act of accepting; the receiving of something offered, with acquiescence, approbation, or satisfaction; especially, favourable reception;

acceptation.e: From Middle English acceptacioun, acceptation, from Middle French acceptacion and Late Latin acceptātiō. By surface analysis, accept + -ation.
acceptation.g: The meaning (sense) in which a word or expression is understood, or generally received.

access.e: From Middle English accesse, acces, borrowed from Middle French acces (“attack, onslaught”) or from its source Latin accessus, perfect passive participle of accēdō (“approach; accede”), from ad (“to, toward, at”) + cēdō (“move, yield”). The sense "entrance" was first attested about 1380.
access.g: A way or means of approaching or entering; an entrance; a passage.

accessory.e: From Medieval Latin accessōrius, from Latin accessor (“helper, subordinate”), from accessus.
accessory.g: Having a secondary, supplementary or subordinate function by accompanying as a subordinate; aiding in a secondary way; being additional; con

accessory.e: From Middle English accessorie, from Medieval Latin accessōrius, from Latin accessor (“helper, subordinate”), from accessus.
accessory.g: Something that belongs to part of another main thing; something additional and subordinate, an attachment.

accommodate.e: First use appears c. the 1530s, borrowed from Latin accommodātus, perfect passive participle of accommodō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + commodō (“to provide, lend; to make fit, accommodate”), from con- + modus (“measure, proportion, limit”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix) (see English mode).
accommodate.g: To render fit, suitable, or correspondent; to adapt.

accompaniment.e: From French accompagnement; equivalent to accompany + -ment.
accompaniment.g: A part, usually performed by instruments, that gives support or adds to the background in music, or adds for ornamentation; also, the harmon

accompany.e: From Middle English accompanien, from Old French acompagner (“to associate with”), from compaing (“companion”), nominative singular of compaignon (“companion”).
accompany.g: To go with or attend as a companion or associate; to keep company with; to go along with.

accomplish.e: From Middle English accomplisshen, acomplissen, from Old French acompliss-, extended stem of acomplir (Modern French accomplir), from Vulgar Latin *(ac)complīre, from Latin complēre (“fill up/out, complete”, whence English complete).

accord.e: From Middle English accord, from Old French acort, from acorder (see verb below).
accord.g: Agreement of opinion, will, or action.

accord.e: From Middle English accorden, acorden, borrowed from Old French acorder (compare modern French accord and accorder), from Vulgar Latin *accordāre, from Latin concordāre via prefix substitution (with Latin ad-), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱḗr ~ *ḱr̥d-, and thus distantly related to English heart (via Proto-Germanic *hertô).
accord.g: To make to agree or correspond; to suit one thing to another; to adjust.

accordance.e: From Middle English accordaunce, from Old French acordance (“agreeing, reconciliation, harmony”).

accordingly.e: From Middle English acordingli, equivalent to according + -ly.

account.e: From Middle English acounte, from Anglo-Norman acunte (“account”), from Old French aconte, from aconter (“to reckon”), from Latin computō (“to sum up”).
account.g: A registry of pecuniary transactions; a written or printed statement of business dealings or debts and credits, and also of other things sub

account.e: From Old French acounter, accomptere et al., from a- + conter (“to count”)).

accountable.g: Obliged, when called upon, to answer (for one’s deeds); answerable.

accurate.e: Borrowed from Latin accūrātus, perfect passive participle of accūrō (“to take care of”), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + cūrō (“care for”).
accurate.g: Telling the truth or giving a true result; exact; not defective or faulty.

accursed.e: From Middle English acursed, from acursen (“to curse”), from Old English ācursian, from ā- + cursian, from curs (“curse”).

accusation.e: Inherited from Middle English accusacion, borrowed from Old French acusacion (French: accusation), from Latin accūsātiō (“accusation, indictment”), from accūsō (“blame, accuse”). Equivalent to accuse + -ation.

accuse.e: From Middle English acusen, from Old French acuser, from Latin accūsō (“to call to account, accuse”), from ad (“to”) + causa (“cause, lawsuit, reason”).
accuse.g: To find fault with, blame, censure.

accused.g: The person charged with an offense; the defendant in a criminal case.

accuser.e: From Middle English acuser, accusour, borrowed from Old French accusour, from Latin accūsātor, from accūsāre. Equivalent to accuse + -er.
accuser.g: One who accuses; one who brings a charge of crime or fault.

ache.e: From Middle English aken (verb), and ache (noun), from Old English acan (verb) (from Proto-West Germanic *akan, from Proto-Germanic *akaną (“to ache”)) and æċe (noun) (from Proto-West Germanic *aki, from Proto-Germanic *akiz), traditionally explained as from a Proto-Indo-European *h₂égos.
ache.g: To suffer pain; to be the source of, or be in, pain, especially continued dull pain; to be distressed.

ache.e: From Middle English ache, from Old French ache, from Latin apium (“celery”). Reinforced by modern French ache.

achieve.e: From Middle English achieven, acheven (“to accomplish (something); to acquire or obtain (something); to carry out or finish (something); to succeed in (something); to happen, turn out”), from Anglo-Norman achever, achiever, Middle French achever, achiever, and Old French achever, achiever (“to accomplish (something); to finish (something).
achieve.g: To carry out or conclude (something, as a task) successfully; to accomplish.

acknowledge.e: Recorded since 1553, a blend of Middle English aknowen (“to recognize, acknowledge”) and knowlechen (“to discover, reveal, acknowledge”). The former verb is from Old English oncnāwan, ācnāwan (“to know, recognize, acknowledge”), from on + cnāwan (“to know”). The latter is derived from the noun at hand in knowledge.
acknowledge.g: To admit the knowledge of; to recognize as a fact or truth; to declare one's belief in.

acquaint.e: From Middle English aqueynten, acointen, from Old French acointier, from Early Medieval Latin accognitāre, from Late Latin accognitus, past participle of accognoscō, from Latin cognoscō, from nōscō.
acquaint.g: To furnish or give experimental knowledge of; to make (one) know; to make familiar.

acquaintance.e: From Middle English aqueyntaunce, from Anglo-Norman aquaintaunce, aqueintance, Old French acointance (“friendship, familiarity”), from Old French acointier (“to acquaint”). Morphologically acquaint + -ance.
acquaintance.g: A state of being acquainted with a person; originally indicating friendship, intimacy, but now suggesting a slight knowledge less deep than

acquire.e: From Middle English acqueren, from Old French aquerre, from Latin acquirō; ad- + quaerō (“to seek for”).

acquit.e: From Middle English aquī̆ten (“to give in return; to pay, repay; to redeem (a pledge, security), to make good (a promise); to make amends; to relieve of an obligation; to acquit, clear of a charge; to free; to deprive of; to do one's part, acquit oneself; to act, behave (in a certain way)”).

acre.e: From Middle English acre, aker, from Old English æcer (“field where crops are grown”), from Proto-West Germanic *akr, from Proto-Germanic *akraz (“field”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵros (“field”).
acre.g: An English unit of land area (symbol: a. or ac.) originally denoting a day's ploughing for a yoke of oxen, now standardized as 4,840 square

across.e: From Middle English acros, from early Middle English a-croiz, a-creoyz, from Anglo-Norman an (“in, on”) + croiz (“in the form of a cross”). By surface analysis, a- + cross.
across.g: To, toward, or from the far side of (something that lies between two points of interest).

act.e: From Middle English acte, from Old French acte, from Latin ācta (“register of events”), plural of āctum (“decree, law”), from agere (“to do, to act”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵeti. Partially displaced deed, from Old English dǣd (“act, deed”).

action.e: From Middle English accioun, accion, from Old French aucion, acciun, from Latin āctiō(n) (“act of doing or making”), from āct(us) + action suffix -iō(n), perfect passive participle of agere (“do, act”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵeti. By surface analysis, act + -ion.
action.g: The effort of performing or doing something.

active.e: From Middle English actyf, from Old French actif, from Latin āctīv(us), from agere (“to do, to act”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵeti. By surface analysis, act + -ive.
active.g: Having the power or quality of acting; causing change; communicating action or motion; acting;—opposed to passive, that receives.

activity.e: From Middle French activité, from Latin activitas. Equivalent to active + -ity.
activity.g: The state or quality of being active; activeness.

actual.e: From Middle English actual, actuel (“active”), from Anglo-Norman actuel, actual, and its source Late Latin actuālis (“active, practical”), from Latin actus (“act, action, performance”), from agere (“to do; to act”) + -alis (“-al”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵeti, from the root *h₂eǵ-. By surface analysis, act + -u- + -al.
actual.g: relating to a person's acts or deeds; active, practical

actually.e: From Middle English actually, actuelly, equivalent to actual + -ly.
actually.g: In act or in fact; really; in truth; positively.

acute.e: From Late Middle English acute (“of a disease or fever: starting suddenly and lasting for a short time; of a humour: irritating, sharp”), from Latin acūta, from acūtus (“sharp, sharpened”), perfect passive participle of acuō (“to make pointed, sharpen, whet”), from acus (“needle, pin”). The word is cognate to ague (“acute, intermittent fever”).
